title: Who is a Sikh
hookLine: the Rehat Maryada defines a Sikh as one who believes in One God, the ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib and the Tenth Guru's amrit
tomorrow: The daily banis, in the code

lines: THE CODE BEGINS WITH A QUESTION.
cards: A hospital intake form has a line that says religion, and a blank about an inch long. One word fits there. But a word in a blank doesn't say what it holds.
A family? A country? A list of rules?

A feeling? Sikhs have a written answer, at the very start of the shared code met in passing with the rehatnamas: the Sikh Rehat Maryada, the code of conduct published by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee.
For the next stretch, the path walks through that code, a piece a day. It begins with a question small enough to fit in the blank. Who is a Sikh?

teach.b: Here is the code's answer, in paraphrase.

teach.h: ONE GOD, TEN GURUS, THE GRANTH.
teach.b: A Sikh is any human being who faithfully believes in one Immortal Being; in the ten Gurus, from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh; in the Guru Granth Sahib; in the words and teachings of the ten Gurus; and in the amrit, the initiation the Tenth Guru gave; and who holds to no other religion as their own.
Start with the first words: any human being. The door isn't marked with a caste, a birthplace, a family name or a language. None of those appear in the list at all.
Then look at what is there. One God. The teachers.
The book where the teaching now lives. The teaching itself. And the Tenth Guru's initiation.

teach.h: BELIEF IN THE TENTH GURU'S AMRIT.
teach.b: On the amrit, the definition asks for belief in the initiation the Tenth Guru gave.

Some readers point out that this leaves room for a person who holds that path as true and has not yet walked through it; the code speaks about those who have taken amrit, and what is asked of them, in its own later sections.
Tradition says a sikh is a learner, a disciple. Read that way, the definition is a learner's list, running in a line from God to the person reading. And notice how short it is.
A child could learn it. A grown person could hold it up against their own life and see where they stand. The code could have opened with rules.
It opens with belief, plainly put, and the rules come after.

how: The Sikh Rehat Maryada opens with a short definition of a Sikh by belief, and Sikh teachers and gurdwara classes often start with it when explaining the code.

games.q: what does “who is a sikh” mean?
o: anyone who wears a turban and speaks Punjabi
any human being who holds the beliefs the code names
a person born into a Sikh family in Punjab

games.q: inside the definition: tap the pairs.
p: the first thing named in the list
Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh
the initiation the Tenth Guru gave

s: the code's definition names a caste or a birthplace
it opens with any human being. caste, birthplace, family name and language don't appear in the list.
the Guru Granth Sahib is in the definition
one God, the ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib, their teachings, and the Tenth Guru's amrit.
the code opens with a list of daily rules
it opens with who a Sikh is, by belief. the daily rules come after.

games.q: a friend asks what makes someone a Sikh. where does the Sikh code begin its answer?
o: with a family name and a birthplace.
with a short list of what a person believes.
with the rules for each hour of the day.
games.why: the code opens with belief: one God, the ten Gurus, the Granth, their teachings and the Tenth Guru's amrit. the rules come later.

practice: Whatever you hold, or are still testing, put it into a few short lines, no big words, nothing borrowed, only what you'd sign your name under today, with a question mark on any line that feels shaky.
Then notice which line feels the most solid.

wordCard.voice: Who is a Sikh. The code's opening answer: any human being who believes in one God, the ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib, their teachings and the Tenth Guru's amrit. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: by tradition, a learner, a disciple, the one who learns from the Guru.

carryVoice: Your line: belief, plainly put. Short enough for a child to learn, and solid enough to stand on. Until tomorrow.
